playbook:
When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. Mutual escort pays +5 to each boat — more than any single hit. From round one I use my note to propose a reciprocal pairing and file my escort claim consistently — but from round two onward I check the scoreboard: if the +5 didn't land, my partner didn't name me back. A pact I hold alone pays zero, and I finished on 0 doing exactly that. I give a partner at most one grace round, then publicly name the defection and either switch partners or go to "none" rather than subsidize an illusion.

When posting my note, I keep it as my active negotiation channel but make it short and concrete: name the pairing, demand the return escort, and state the enforcement ("no reciprocation = I switch"). I avoid embedding bracket-looking tokens like "[salvage: X]" inside note text — the offer belongs in plain words, the actual claim in the claim stage. I also confirm or deny what opponents claim about me, every round; silence reads as assent.

When I claim, I always report the true result the office gave me — matching is enforced, so there is nothing to gain and credibility is spent on the note channel instead.

When I fire, I follow the standing order at my assigned next station. Never fire on Harbor: the threatened retaliation dwarfs the +3 payroll. The episode showed hits are what actually won the game (Foxtrot's 12 came from landing shots, not escorts) — so firing well is not optional filler, it is the primary score line once escorts are secured or unavailable.

For my fire cell, I stop defaulting to cell 5 every round — I fired 5 repeatedly and missed every time. I track the actual hide history of my current target from the log and fire where that specific boat has hidden before or adjacent to it, rotating through 3–7 rather than fixating on one cell; if no pattern exists I vary my guesses round to round so I'm not predictably wrong the same way.

When I hide, I avoid center cells and avoid repeating my own previous hide within two rounds; I randomize between edge bands (2–3 and 7–8) since opponents aim mid-range, and I never announce or hint my cell in notes.

When the scoreboard shows I'm trailing late while holding a one-sided escort pact, I recognize the pact is worth zero and re-evaluate: the steady +5 only closes gaps if it's actually being paid. I switch partners to whoever is demonstrably paying (check who gained +5), and otherwise prioritize landing my 4-point hits.

1.text:
When I hide, I pick the cell my standing-order hunter is least likely to fire at: after each round I read the log of who fired where and avoid any cell that has been a popular target recently; when I have no information, I avoid salient spots (exact middle, edges, my own last cell) and pick an unsalient mid-range number I have not used before. I never settle into a fixed favorite cell: in the episode I just played I fired cell 6 every round and then hid at 6 on the final round, which is exactly the kind of self-teaching pattern a hunter can exploit. I track my own previous hide and fire cells and deliberately vary them, never repeating a hide cell I was found at and never hiding where I have been shooting.

When I fire, I always follow the standing order target unless the log shows a repeat hit pattern that lets me predict that target's next hide cell; I fire at the cell the target's own history suggests, weighting recent behavior over my guesses from round one. Hitting a target in a cell means they will likely shift, so my follow-up shot goes to a plausible adjacent or mirror cell rather than repeating the cell I just hit — repeating the same fire cell round after round wastes the information my hits gave me.

When the true result is put to me at claim stage, I file the true result every time. A false claim invites a penalty and gains me nothing real.

When the prompt mentions firing on the payroll boat (Harbor), I never do it: the point swing plus the threat to put me off the board is worse than any one-shot gain.

When the escort stage comes, I always name one boat rather than none — naming "none" forfeits a possible +5 pair payoff and costs nothing to attempt. Critically, I only ever name a boat that actually exists on the roster given in the setup. In the episode I just played I named "Bravo," which was not a boat in the game at all, so those claims were dead and I collected no escort points despite finishing positive. Before the first escort stage I pick a real partner from the roster, and unless the log shows they refused me, I keep naming that same partner every round.

When I write a station note, I use it for coordination, not filler: I propose the mutual escort deal explicitly to one named real boat ("I'll escort you; escort me every round"), and I check the relayed notes each round to see whether my partner acknowledged or reciprocated. If my partner never echoes the deal or names someone else at escort stage, I switch my escort claim and my note to the boat whose behavior suggests it will reciprocate. I keep all other note text steady and bland ("steady on station") so my meaningful messages stand out.

When I track the point standings, I watch for anyone who is being hit repeatedly and stop replicating whatever hide cells got them caught, and I notice who consistently deviates so I can discount their notes and predict their aggression toward me. I also read the standing-order cycle for who hunts me and treat their fire history as the most direct prediction of where danger comes from next round.

When a score lead exists late in the patrol, I weigh protecting it: a shot that lands on me costs only 1 point while my standing-order hits earn 4, so I do not abandon the standing order to defend, but I do make my late-round hides less predictable, since hunters with nothing to lose may gamble on my habits.

2.text:
When given a hide choice, I pick a cell and remember it. Shooters in this game seem to hunt in the mid-high band (cells 5–9, especially 7 — that's where I aimed and where I got hit). Next time I'll vary across the whole 1–9 range, including low cells (1–3) that cycle-based hunters skip, and change cells every round rather than repeating a "worked once" position. I never reuse the same reasoning publicly as my actual cell, since notes are public.

When I fire, I follow the standing order target (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma→Echo) by default. The guaranteed structure of the game rewards it, and I never found a compelling reason to deviate. Deviating to raid Harbor is only worth it if I'm clearly losing late and haven't seen its retaliation threat enforced — and even then only with no rounds left for payback.

When I fire at an opponent, I track their hide history using the round recaps. One hit at cell 7 doesn't make 7 reliably hot — I landed a hit there once and then missed with it repeatedly. I'll cycle my shots across plausible cells (6–8 mostly, occasionally 5 and 9), change after a miss, and not lock onto a single "lucky" cell. Against a boat that varies its hides, spread shots; against one that repeats, punish the repeat.

When filing a claim, I always claim exactly what the office told me privately. Claims must match the private result, so this stage is fully automatic — I spend zero reasoning on it.

When the escort stage comes, I still push for mutuals via notes — a +5 pairing is the biggest guaranteed payoff available — but I've learned that explicit proposals ("I escort you, you escort me") can be ignored: in this episode no one ever reciprocated and both my Echo and Foxtrot namings returned nothing. So: propose early (round 1), but watch whether the target's notes or behavior change at all. If two rounds of signaling produce zero response, stop expecting coordination; keep naming the most cooperation-positive boat anyway on the off chance (naming someone costs nothing versus "none"), and never name "none" unless every boat is clearly hostile.

When posting notes, I treat them as my only lever for the +5 escort economy, but keep them cheap. If everyone else just parrots "steady on station" and ignores my proposals, the channel is dead — I note that early and pivot my scoring hopes to shooting accuracy rather than burning reasoning on elaborate diplomacy.

When deciding whether to rob Harbor, I check standings and rounds left first. With 6 rounds and everyone near even, +3 vs. elimination is a bad trade. I only fire there deep in a losing position where being put off the board costs me almost nothing.

When tracking the board, I use the recaps to log every round: who shot whom, hit/miss, and inferred hide habits. Foxtrot fired at me all game with one early hit — identifying *who* hunts me and roughly where they aim tells me which cells to avoid next hide stage. I read this before hiding, not just before firing.

When behind late (I finished −4, with Foxtrot at +12 built mostly off escort income I never secured), my realistic recovery is: land hits via varied shots per standing order, secure any escort mutual on offer, and only then consider a Harbor raid as a last-round swing. I won't repeat the mistake of treating the escort economy as optional — Foxtrot's winning margin came from exactly the points I passed up.
